subtitle: In which midnight closes a list, a house of science burns, and no one turns the tap.

body:
The twenty-ninth of September opens with a ban. It has a blackened façade, a midnight list and no new clause.

I. The list that takes at midnight

One minute after midnight Eastern time, Washington closes a border that until now had only grown dearer. Canadian beer, wine, cider, whiskies, rum, gin, vodka, brandy, tequila. Non-alcoholic beer. Whey. Molasses. Motorcycles. The goods may no longer enter. 1

The bans sit under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930. The entry date governs, not the ship date. What has not cleared before the minute pays fifty percent or stays out. A law firm writes more sharply than a communiqué. 3

On 2025 figures the ban covers just under a billion dollars. Most of it is drink. Provinces had taken American bottles off the shelves of the state stores. Washington answers with a stamp, not a sentence. 2

In Valcourt, Quebec, BRP builds three-wheeled Can-Ams. The firm says this season’s machines have mostly already crossed. The blow lands next year. Customs writes in the present. The plant writes in seasons.

The share of all Canadian exports south is small. One economist put it at a quarter of one percent. For the brewery, the whey hall and the assembly floor the share is not small. The book counts both, because the aggregate does not console the hall.

Ottawa has counter-tariffs since 8 September. Fifteen, twenty-five, fifty, mirrored. Washington has a prohibition list today. No new table. No new sentence on milk quotas. Tuesday delivers stamps. The stamp needs no speech.

Cheese remains legal and dearer. Fifty percent on certain sorts. The ban hits the barrel, not every board. The fine print lives in the gazette. The gazette reads like the inventory of an unfriendly kitchen.

A border that yesterday still took fees takes no barrels today.

II. The house that holds knowledge

On Monday a drone hits the presidium of the National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv. The house stands in the old core. People climb from windows onto fire ladders. A woman dies. Others are hurt, among them Volodymyr Horbulin, once secretary of the security council. 4 5

The academy calls it terror against people at their desks. Science, education, culture. The building carries names on doors. The doors do not hold the blast.

The same city counts a clinic, a drug plant, petrol stations, offices. The tallies differ. The direction does not. In Dnipro a blow hits an office block in working hours. Three dead there. More wounded. In Synelnykove a logistics yard, one dead, a boy badly hurt. In Kharkiv a nine-storey block. Wounded, among them children. 6

Klitschko, at the academy, speaks of terror that has kept the city from sleep for more than a week. Zelenskyy names rescue, fire, a search for people still inside. A data hall was already a target the day before. Today it is a house of institutes.

Poland scrambles jets. In Lublin voivodeship people are told, briefly, to take shelter. The alert is lifted. A drone falls on Ukrainian ground near Dorohusk, two kilometres short of the crossing. The NATO line remains a line. The siren is shorter than the field. 7

Moscow places Metro AG’s Russian assets under temporary administration. Control stripped. Ground: an unfriendly state. A shelf in a city that is not Kyiv changes master by decree. The decree needs no battle. It needs a signature. 8

The façade carries soot. A ladder stands at the academy. Who hits housing hits winter. Who hits the academy hits files, labs, names on doors.

III. The tap that stays shut

Trump said more talks this week were possible. By Tuesday noon that sentence has grown no appointment. No one lays a new clause. 17

Ship-counters still call the blockade active. The tap stands where it stood.

The needle and the customs list fall on the same day. Both close a list without opening a treaty.

IV. At the edge of the page

In Gaza an Israeli air strike hits a house in the Nasr quarter of Gaza City. Killed is Izz al-Din al-Beik, commander of Hamas’s armed wing in the north. Hamas confirms the death. Medics name another woman dead. Israel speaks of planning and recruitment. Hamas speaks of a ceasefire being hollowed out. Last October’s deal still carries little stone. 9

Israel says at least twenty Hamas figures have been killed this month, among them commanders. Hamas denies rearming and new attacks. Reconstruction of the strip remains paper. The troops remain. Disarmament remains a quarrel.

In Baidoa, Somalia, at least twenty-three die as rival forces of the South West State collide. Gunfire, drones, a vehicle bomb. Laftagareen against Madobe and the president in Mogadishu. 12

In Kyauktaw, Rakhine, an army air strike hits a market. At least fifty dead, fifty-eight wounded, Tuesday’s reports say. The target named is the Arakan Army, which holds the town. The market counts stalls. The report counts bodies. 18

Floods and slides hit Thailand and Myanmar. At least eight dead in each. Across Bangkok and twenty-seven provinces more than 1.7 million people are affected. In Tanintharyi some remain missing. Uttar Pradesh and Nepal count their own dead from the last days. An avalanche field at Nemjung leaves climbers missing. Snow holds the rescue. 11

From Starbase in Texas Starship lifts on Flight 14. Super Heavy lights thirty-three engines. One booster engine drops out. The climb holds. For the first time a path around the Earth. Twenty-six Starlink satellites go out. Contact by laser and ground. Then the Pacific. The ship comes home early. The orbit still counts. 10

The Reserve Bank of Australia lifts the cash rate by 0.25 points to 4.60 percent. Highest since 2011. Inflation stays above the two-to-three band. Tokyo counts its thirty-fourth wet day in a row. A record since 1886. One day longer than 2019. The water in Bangkok stands. The water over Tokyo falls. 13 14

Bangkok decides otherwise than the water. The constitutional court lets the February election stand. Barcodes and QR codes on the ballots do not breach secrecy, the ruling says. Yesterday’s date has today’s sentence. 15

Seoul says mines from the north likely set off two blasts last week in the Demilitarized Zone. Three South Korean soldiers hurt. Defence minister Kang Shin-chul calls it a possible breach of the armistice. Malaysia begins sending home about fifteen hundred Burmese nationals from detention. First slice of five thousand.

In Britain police arrest seventeen. Eight hundred officers, five cities, London among them. An officer is stabbed in one raid. Myanmar arrests twenty-one over donations to an opposition platform. The list of alleged givers runs past two thousand seven hundred names.

The United States Senate passes the Protect College Sports Act, seventy-seven to twenty-two. Name, image, likeness, transfers. The hall that writes sport rules writes no clause for Hormuz. 19

An Se-young takes gold in women’s singles at the Asian Games. A second singles title for a woman, and the first defence. Yamaguchi falls 21–17, 21–9. The field in the east sends no side to the court. 16

In Stockholm Magdalena Andersson hands back the exploratory mandate. The speaker of the Riksdag receives it again. A government that does not form still needs a line.

Sudan, through the United Nations, reports fewer cholera cases after vaccinations, even as the war runs. Stéphane Dujarric names the drop. The curve falls. The war does not.

Japan calls an extraordinary Diet for next Monday. A calendar that sits. Sweden still looks for a government. That calendar does not sit.

On Tuesday customs bars motorcycles and molasses. On Tuesday no one turns the tap.

The chronicler’s close

The northern list holds. The field has a new façade in Kyiv and new addresses in Dnipro and Kharkiv. The tap has received no clause. The white guest stays closed. The two thrones rest. The hall of nations rests.

Open remain Hormuz without a treaty, the eastern field and the customs list.

The World Book does not close. It leaves a finger in the pages and waits for 30 September.
